transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-12
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 75 minutes (scheduled)
Attendees: Jamie Park (Redwood AE), Ravi Menon (Redwood SE), Clara Liu (Redwood Solutions Eng); Evelyn Hart (Meridian CTO), Diego Alvarez (ML Platform Lead), Priya Kapoor (Infra Eng), Samir Chaudhry (Security)
Recording: auto transcript (medium quality)
Summary:
Quick lab-style workshop to align on an apples-to-apples benchmark protocol for Meridian's on-prem/private VPC rollout. Focus on: how we generate load (replay vs synthetic), how to represent cold-cache vs steady-state, kv cache warmup heuristics, and quantization profiles that preserve the production prompt set. Agreed next steps and owners.
---
Topics covered:
- Overall benchmarking goals and success criteria
- Prompt set selection and sequence-length distribution
- Replay capture methodology vs synthetic generator parameters
- KV-cache warmup and TTL semantics (prefix caching behavior)
- Batching strategy, concurrency targets, and continuous batching effects
- Quantization tradeoffs (4-bit/8-bit) and regression testing
- Security/VPC constraints for on-prem runs
---
Action items (captured in notes): see action_items field above.
---
Transcript:
[00:00] Jamie Park: Okay folks, thanks for joining. We'll run about 75 minutes, go deep on the load fidelity lab and leave with concrete next steps. Evelyn, want to kick off with your goals?
[00:12] Evelyn Hart: Sure. Thanks Jamie. High level, Meridian needs to validate that when we move our inference into a private cluster the P90 latency stays under 220ms for our customer-facing prompts and cost per 1M tokens doesn't jump more than 30%. We're also concerned about tail latency during burst.
[00:30] Diego Alvarez: And to add, we have a mix — 60% short prompts (<=64 tokens), 30% mid (65-256), 10% long (>256). But those long ones are critical for support summarization. We want apples-to-apples comparisons across GPU SKUs and quantization modes.
[00:45] Ravi Menon: Got it. We'll need to be careful about sequence length distribution in the generator. If you already have a historical request trace, the best is replay with time-of-day patterns. But replay has privacy bits, so we suggested sampling and redaction in the capture.
[01:05] Priya Kapoor: We can provide a sanitized trace. But curious about the cold-cache vs warm-cache windows: how long after a scale-up do you expect KV cache to be effective?
[01:18] Clara Liu: There's a couple of knobs. By default Redwood's runtime uses per-worker KV cache that populates on first generation. For our benchmarks we typically model three phases: cold (empty cache), warmup (simulate real traffic until prefix cache hits stabilize), and steady-state. Warmup time depends a lot on your prompt variety and prefix overlap. In our experience with customer fleets, 10-30 minutes of realistic traffic often stabilizes cache hit rate for short-response workloads.
[01:45] Samir Chaudhry: Quick security note — the VPC/on-prem runs need to keep customer PII out of logs. We'll need to confirm what Redwood collects by default.
[01:54] Jamie Park: We can share our telemetry spec; by default we capture token counts, per-request latency, and anonymized prompt hash. No raw prompt storage unless you opt in. We'll attach the security doc.
[02:10] Diego Alvarez: On quantization: we plan to try 8-bit and 4-bit. The worry is hallucination increase on longer prompts. What's your recommended regression test?
[02:20] Ravi Menon: Two pronged — automated quality metrics and human eval. For automated, run pairwise BLEU/ROUGE-style similarity on deterministic tasks and embedding distance on semantic tasks. Also run a small suite of seeded prompts where we know expected output tokens; that's our canary. For hallucinations, our 'golden examples' are the most telling.
[02:40] Evelyn Hart: Can you also standardize temperature and top_k/top_p? We need identical decoding parameters across runs.
[02:46] Clara Liu: Absolutely. We lock sampling seeds where possible; for nondeterministic decoders we run large sample sizes and compare distributions. We'll include a config file with decoding params pinned.
[03:00] Priya Kapoor: On load generation: we prefer replay but if we sample we lose timing characteristics. Do you have a synthetic generator that can replicate diurnal spikes and user think time?
[03:12] Ravi Menon: Yes, our load runner supports inter-arrival distributions (Poisson, Weibull) and can replay original timestamps after anonymization. For apples-to-apples GPU comparisons, we also recommend a hybrid approach: replay core production flows for fidelity and synthetic bursts to test headroom.
[03:34] Diego Alvarez: How do you handle KV cache pre-warming for replay? If we replay identical requests, the cache will be hot immediately which hides cold-start behavior.
[03:42] Clara Liu: Two strategies: 1) Time-shifted replay where you stagger identical sessions across workers so initial requests hit empty caches; or 2) insert cold windows — e.g., drain workers and start replay after ramp to measure cold P95 separately. We can automate both.
[04:05] Evelyn Hart: Let's make sure our SLA validation includes both scenarios. We want to know both cold P95 and warm P95.
[04:12] Jamie Park: Agreed. We'll include a canonical experiment matrix in the repo.
[04:18] Samir Chaudhry: Network egress and private link: our security team requires that Redwood's test runner be deployed inside our VPC or over a private peering. How is that handled?
[04:28] Ravi Menon: For private deployments we offer two paths: 1) Redwood runs an ephemeral agent inside your VPC (customer-managed) that executes the workload and uploads aggregated metrics; or 2) you run the runner entirely and we provide the config and dashboards. For compliance, option 2 is what most FSI customers pick.
[04:48] Priya Kapoor: We'll likely go with option 2. We prefer to keep traffic internal. We'll need the runner image and a sample k8s job manifest.
[04:56] Clara Liu: We'll push a helm chart and a container image that runs the replay and synthetic generators. It supports multi-node coordination and KV cache warming protocols (we tag sessions so cache warming can be observed).
[05:12] Diego Alvarez: On metrics — what exactly do you collect? We need per-model latency histograms, per-token breakdown, cache hit ratios, GPU utilization, and memory pressure. Also bucketed by sequence length.
[05:25] Ravi Menon: Yes: per-request start/end, token counts, per-layer kernel timing (where available), KV cache hit/miss, batch sizes, GPU utilization (nvidia-smi export), and scheduling stalls. We'll standardize histogram buckets.
[05:40] Evelyn Hart: Who owns the canonical prompt set? We want to ensure it's reproducible and versioned.
[05:45] Jamie Park: We'll put the seed prompt set in the repo as a versioned CSV and tag each benchmark run with a commit hash. The prompt set should be a mix: 50% sampled recent traffic (sanitized), 30% edge-long prompts, 20% synthetic corner-case prompts.
[06:03] Priya Kapoor: For quantization testing, can you run cross-model comparisons? E.g., same model in fp16 on sku A vs int4 on sku B? We need unit-cost normalization.
[06:14] Ravi Menon: Yes, we normalize by tokens per dollar and also by tokens per second per GPU. We produce an efficiency matrix: latency vs cost, and a fallback matrix showing quality regressions at each quant level.
[06:30] Clara Liu: One caveat: different kernels and attention implementations can change output bit-for-bit. For strict apples-to-apples we recommend locking runtime versions and kernel libraries. We'll supply a baseline docker image and exact driver/kernel notes.
[06:46] Diego Alvarez: If we lock runtime versions, we're worried about not testing the latest optimizations. But for comparison that's necessary.
[06:53] Ravi Menon: Right — baseline runs should lock to the same runtime. Then run a separate 'opt' test that includes newer kernels to measure gains. Keep both sets.
[07:04] Evelyn Hart: Are there known issues with 4-bit quant and long context?
[07:09] Clara Liu: The biggest issue is accumulation noise on long histories. We often see small token-level divergences that compound on >1k token sequences. That's why we do semantic similarity checks, not raw token equality.
[07:22] Samir Chaudhry: Any PII leakage risk during replay? Make sure redaction is robust.
[07:27] Jamie Park: We'll include a scrubber (regex + ML-based redactor) in the capture pipeline. If you prefer, you can run capture and scrub locally and only share hashes and metadata.
[07:40] Diego Alvarez: For the actual lab config, can you share an example experiment matrix? We need explicit rows like: GPU_Sku, Quant_Mode, Batch_Max, Concurrency_Target, Warmup_Duration, Run_Length, Seed_Set_Hash.
[07:53] Ravi Menon: Yes — we'll publish a CSV template. Example row: A100-80GB, fp16, batch_max 32, concurrency 200, warmup 30m, run_length 4h, seed_hash abc123.
[08:05] Priya Kapoor: Let's talk about continuous batching: if the runtime aggregates across requests to improve throughput, it can increase tail latency. Can we measure the batching distribution?
[08:15] Clara Liu: We capture observed batch size per generation and correlate with latency. We can also force a no-batching run to see the baseline. We recommend both. For production-like runs, enable batching and measure the tradeoffs.
[08:30] Evelyn Hart: How do we account for autoscaling events? They can cause cold starts and noisier metrics.
[08:36] Ravi Menon: We run structured tests: fixed capacity (no autoscale), autoscale with defined policies, and stress bursts to trigger scale. Each is a column in the results.
[08:48] Diego Alvarez: About telemetry: can we get raw histograms to import into our observability?
[08:53] Jamie Park: Yes, we push prometheus-compatible exports and raw CSVs.
[08:59] Samir Chaudhry: Any legal constraints for sharing kernel-level timings with third-party vendors?
[09:04] Jamie Park: We usually share aggregated kernel timing; if you need raw traces we can sign an NDA addendum.
[09:12] Diego Alvarez: One operational question — when measuring cost, do you include network egress in tokens-per-dollar? For on-prem it's different.
[09:19] Ravi Menon: We separate cost components: compute, storage, network. For on-prem we estimate amortized hardware costs; for cloud we use actual SKU pricing. We'll provide a cost breakdown spreadsheet.
[09:32] Priya Kapoor: Great. If we run the 48h replay, we should include a controlled incident window to see behaviour under node loss. Can Redwood simulate node-preemption?
[09:41] Clara Liu: Yes. We can create failure injection hooks to kill a worker and observe failover and fallback to larger models if configured. We'll include chaos scenarios.
[09:52] Evelyn Hart: Okay let's recap next steps so responsibilities are clear.
[09:57] Jamie Park: Ravi will publish the load repo including examples and the experiment matrix by 11/16. Priya will stand up VPC and share runner access by 11/20. Evelyn will provide the top-10 golden prompts and acceptance criteria by 11/18. Joint run of 48h replay targeted for completion 11/30.
[10:20] Diego Alvarez: We'll also want a checklist for the security review — SSO keys, audit log retention, and KMS integrations.
[10:28] Samir Chaudhry: I'll coordinate with Redwood's security contact after we get the docs.
[10:35] Jamie Park: Perfect. We'll follow up with the repo link, helm chart, and the security appendix.
[10:40] Clara Liu: Quick note — when you scrub prompts, keep a small set of unsanitized golden prompts local to you for human eval; those don't need to be shared.
[10:49] Evelyn Hart: Makes sense. Thanks everyone. That was productive.
[10:54] Jamie Park: Thanks — we'll send notes and links. Closing in 5.
[11:00] (end recording)
